title: No merit
hookLine: an emperor lists his temples and asks what merit he has made; Bodhidharma says none

cards: Temples built. Sutras copied. Monks and nuns supported.
Offerings given. That's the list an emperor brings, in the old Chan story, to the strange monk from India.

The emperor is Wu of Liang, a ruler devoted to Buddhism, and he wants to know one thing: after all this, how much merit have I made? It's a fair question, the kind a person asks after years of doing good.
And Bodhidharma's answer is short. No merit.

teach.b: Merit, in Buddhist teaching, is the good that comes from good actions, and Buddhist texts speak of making it by giving, by supporting monks and by building places to practice.

The emperor was doing exactly that, so the answer stings. Second, how the Platform Sutra explains it. In that text a local official, puzzled by the story, asks the teacher Huineng what Bodhidharma meant.
Huineng says the emperor's building and giving bring blessings, good fortune, and that's real.
But merit in the deeper sense, he says, is something else: seeing your own true nature, and treating everyone with the same humble respect. It isn't stored up like grain in a barn.
It's found inside, in how you see and how you act. Third, another telling. The Blue Cliff Record, a later book of Chan stories, opens with a different version of the meeting.
There the emperor asks, what is the highest meaning of the holy truths?
Bodhidharma answers: vast emptiness, nothing holy. The emperor asks, then who is standing in front of me? Bodhidharma says: I don't know.
The emperor doesn't understand, and Bodhidharma leaves and crosses the river north. Fourth, what the story aims at.
It doesn't say giving is foolish; Huineng says it brings blessings.

It aims at the ledger, the quiet counting in the back of the mind. A kindness done while keeping score is still a kindness. The Chan question is what it would feel like with no scoreboard running at all.

how: Making merit through giving and service is part of Buddhist life in many forms, and some Chan and Zen teachers retell the Emperor Wu story as a warning against keeping score.

o: a teaching that giving to temples is pointless
a jab at keeping score, not at giving itself
a rule that monks may not accept offerings

p: blessings are not the same as merit

s: the story says building temples is worthless
Huineng says giving brings blessings; the story aims at the counting.
in the Blue Cliff Record, Bodhidharma says 'I don't know'

Huineng explains the story in the Platform Sutra

games.q: you're Bodhidharma. an emperor who has built temples and fed monks asks how much merit he's made. what do you say?
o: a great deal, more than anyone.
games.why: Bodhidharma said no merit. in the Platform Sutra, Huineng explains: the giving brings blessings, but merit is in seeing your own nature.

practice: Bring to mind something kind you did recently, and notice whether a little scoreboard lights up: that was good of me, they owe me one. Don't scold it; just see it, and let the number fade.
Then rest with the breath, holding lightly the thought of a small good thing no one would ever know was you.

wordCard.voice: No merit. Bodhidharma's short answer to an emperor's list, aimed not at giving but at the counting.

orig.note: Sanskrit: merit, the good that comes from good actions; Pali puñña.

carryVoice: Your line: a kindness with no scoreboard. Giving still brings blessings; only the ledger is in question. See you tomorrow.
